variants.name: C++20 std::stop_token and std::jthread
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 stores the request in the standard library: std::stop_source owns the stop-state and is the only trigger, std::stop_token is the thread-safe read-only view passed to each operation, and std::jthread injects the token into its callable and calls request_stop() in its destructor before joining. Waits become interruptible through std::condition_variable_any::wait(lock, token, pred), and std::stop_callback registers a reaction that runs on the thread that calls request_stop(). Use this whenever the toolchain is C++20; pre-C++20 code keeps the manual atomic flag, and Asio-based I/O uses per-operation cancellation instead.
pitfalls: The stop-state lives as long as any token or callback references it, but once the stop_source is destroyed no further request can be made - tokens then report stop_possible() == false; keep the source alive for the whole operation it cancels.

std::stop_callback runs on the thread that calls request_stop(): keep the callback short and non-blocking, and never destroy a callback (or its token) from inside another callback, since that blocks until the running one returns.
Polling only between large units of work gives no cancellation latency: check the token around each blocking step and prefer interruptible waits over fixed sleeps.
condition_variable_any::wait(lock, token, pred) can return because of a stop request, not only because the predicate became true - check the predicate (or the token) before using the data.

variants.name: Pre-C++20 std::atomic flag polling
variants.idiom_name: std::atomic<bool> token shared by reference, checked at safe points
variants.implementation_notes: Before C++20 the token is hand-written: one std::atomic<bool> (or atomic_flag) owned by the requester and captured by reference or shared_ptr in every operation, with a condition_variable or timed waits so blocked workers wake and re-check. This is the classic form of the pattern in C++ and remains justified when the ABI is frozen, when the token must cross a C boundary, or when a shared_ptr control block is cheaper than a stop-state. Migration to stop_token is mechanical: the flag becomes std::stop_source and the checks become stop_requested().
pitfalls: A relaxed atomic is enough for the flag itself, but the data published together with the cancellation needs its own synchronisation; do not assume the flag orders anything.
Waiting without a timeout on a condition variable makes the request invisible until the predicate changes: use wait_for/wait_until and re-check the flag in the predicate loop.
Capturing the flag by reference into a thread that outlives the scope is a dangling reference; own it in a shared_ptr or keep it in a scope that provably outlives every worker.

variants.name: Boost.Asio per-operation cancellation
variants.implementation_notes: For asynchronous I/O on Asio, cancellation is per operation rather than per call tree: a cancellation_signal has a single slot, emit() invokes the slot's handler, and the handler cancels exactly the async operation it was bound to. Bind the slot to an operation through bind_cancellation_slot, or hand the signal to composed operations that propagate it to their inner steps. This is the right tool when the thing to stop is an outstanding async_accept/async_read/async_wait rather than a loop; keep an application-level token for the surrounding task lifetime and let the signal do the I/O-level stopping.
pitfalls: A cancellation_signal has one slot: emitting it after the slot was rebound cancels the wrong operation, so keep one signal per outstanding operation (or hand it to a composed operation that owns the binding).

Cancellation type matters: terminal/partial/total have different effects on composed operations, and an operation may complete successfully before the request is observed - always handle operation_aborted as a normal outcome.
The signal, the socket and the completion handler must outlive the async operation; an emit after the operation completed is a no-op, not an error.
